entries.title: Hardener: an autonomous behavior-review campaign that replaces crucible
entries.brief: Parked by the operator: settle the Tenter/Hardener design and build the campaign that runs a live-substrate module in a sandbox until it converges
entries.body:
## Goal

Replace `crucible`, the hand-run review-and-fix loop, with `Hardener`.
Hardener is an on-demand campaign after loom that runs a live-substrate module in a sandbox, reviews its behavior round after round, and fixes what it finds until the gates are green.
Then retire `crucible/`, which still writes to `_mill/` and runs its rounds through hand-spawned `crucible-reviewer-<effort>` agents.

## Starting point

- The design under `## Design` (DRAFT): `Tenter` is the round loop on `Treadle`, and `Hardener` is `Shed` wrapping `Tenter` with its own Preflight.
  Rounds respawn every time instead of keeping a persistent thread, and a `progress-judge` runs before and after each round.
- `crucible/README.md` is the method Hardener automates.

## Open before Discussion

- What the handoff must carry losslessly besides the finding-recurrence ledger.
- Where the line falls between the Go scaffolding and the LLM's orchestrator role.
- Whether the round agent reuses the `burler` package or only its prompt template.
- How much of the sandbox provisioning lym automates.

## Done when

- `lym` can start a Hardener campaign against a module and run it unattended to convergence or a round cap.
- `crucible/` is deleted, and the design's durable content lives in package docs.

## Notes

- One of the Someday items on `manifest-retire`'s triage list (`hardener`). Landing this entry removes it from that list.

## Design

> **⚠️ DRAFT. This is an early concept sketch, not a settled design.** Unlike the other module docs (which are *Design — not built* but agreed), this one is still being figured out. The shape below captures what a weekend of hand-running the method taught us and the decisions reached so far in discussion; **expect fields, mechanisms, and even the boundary of the module to change.** Do not implement from this doc yet. When the concept firms up this banner comes off and the doc becomes a normal *Design — not built* entry; per the documentation lifecycle it is eventually deleted into the package header + `overview.md` on landing.
>
> **Hand-executed origin:** `crucible` is the method this module would automate — the hand-run version of the same idea, named separately to avoid colliding with this module's own name. This was developed over the last week out of a concrete need: to **run** actual `reed` code hard enough to surface defects a green `go test` never proves. Six hand-orchestrated rounds fixed what many rounds of text-based review could not — it was genuinely *hardening*.
>
> Not required to get `loom` running — `loom` only ever uses text-review (its `Bouncer`+`Burler` review segments), never behavior-review. Kept separate from the `Treadle`/`Shed` work for exactly that reason: nothing here blocks `loom`.

## Naming: two things, not one

Two distinct layers, split out once the shared-engine design (the `internal/treadleengine` and `internal/shedengine` package documentation) was pinned:

- **`Tenter`** — the review-loop alone: `Treadle` (the generic round-loop engine — judge, gate, round-spawn, cap, pause, lock) configured with a live-substrate-driving round-runner and a behavior-review profile, instead of a `burlerengine` round + text-review profile.
  The direct structural sibling of loom's own text-review segments.
  Not separately runnable in isolation the simple way a text-review segment is, because behavior-review needs a live sandbox/worktree lifecycle around it.
- **`Hardener`** — the full, on-demand, autonomous campaign: `Shed` (the generic outer phase-FSM — see `internal/shedengine`'s package documentation) wrapping `Tenter`, plus Hardener's own Preflight (sandbox provisioning, live-suite readiness).
  This is what gets a worktree spawned for it (via `fabric`) and safe-merges back into parent when done, the same lifecycle `loom` uses, just with `Hardener`'s own producer list carrying `Tenter` where `loom`'s list carries its Discussion, Plan and Webster producers.

`Tenter` is a **behavior-based reviewer**: where a text-review segment reads an artifact, `Tenter` **runs** a live-substrate module, reacts to what it observes, and builds bespoke adversarial scenarios to break it. `Hardener` is a separate, on-demand, **post-loom** campaign — not on the `shuttle → burler → shed → loom` spine — meant to harden a live-substrate module (the archetype: `reed` driving real tmux) before merge.

## Why `Tenter` is not a text-review segment

`Tenter` and a text-review segment share the `burler` *round discipline* (see the `internal/burlerengine` package documentation) — A-review → B-fix, no self-grading, commit-per-fix, fix-everything — but they are different reviewers along two axes:

| | text-review segment | `Tenter` |
|---|---|---|
| Mode | **text** — read the artifact | **behavior** — run the module, react, build scenarios |
| Substrate | in-worktree, fast | a **live sandbox repo**; slow, heavy git/go operations |
| Gate | LLM verdict (or a light `command` gate) | **deterministic**: run the smoke suite N× concurrent, zero stray state |
| Cost | cheap, minutes | token- **and** wall-clock-heavy; a single iteration ran 1–2 hours; a campaign, a weekend |
| When | between every phase (on the spine) | **on demand, after loom**, only when `Hardener` is invoked |

A text-review segment's `command` gate lets a code profile *touch* behavior lightly;
`Tenter` is the heavy tier — driving real substrate and hand-rolling crash/rebirth/concurrency scenarios is its whole job.

## `Tenter`'s round-loop — resolved: `Treadle` drives per-round respawn, no persistent thread

**The engine underneath `Tenter` is a general one, not Tenter-specific — see the `internal/treadleengine` package documentation.**
That doc covers the round-runner interface, the judge-maintained handoff (a general improvement, not just Tenter's),
and the process for getting there (`Tenter` itself is built on `Treadle` only once `Treadle` exists).
What follows here is Tenter's own instance of that shared design.

In the hand-run version (see crucible/README.md), **one persistent orchestrator thread** stayed alive across the campaign: it spawned a fresh round agent per round, **independently verified** the round's work (re-ran the gates from cold state on the committed tree — never trusting the round's own "merge-ready" verdict), **accumulated** an understanding of where the module's bugs live, **targeted** each next round agent ("focus on X"), maintained a **handoff** that survived compaction, and asked the operator what to do next.
The targeting + accumulation is what made the reed campaign's rounds succeed where stateless text-review rounds did not — the round agent kept re-discovering the terrain cold otherwise.

**Resolved: no persistent thread.**
Go itself is the orchestrator (`Treadle`);
each round is three fresh, one-shot spawns, not a living session accumulating state in a context window:

1. **`progress-judge`, pre-round.** `Treadle` spawns a fresh one-shot agent that reads the handoff file, decides what to target next, and writes the round's seed prompt (the file the reviewer will read).
   It then terminates — no lingering session.
2. **Reviewer.** `Treadle` spawns the round agent proper, pointed at the prompt the judge just wrote — the same A-review → B-fix, commit-per-fix, no-self-grading round crucible already runs by hand.
   This is the `burler`-shaped worker;
   the *campaign* loop wrapping it is new, the round itself is not.
3. **`progress-judge`, post-round.** `Treadle` spawns a fresh one-shot agent that reads the handoff plus the round's review/fixer-report artifacts, **independently validates the findings** (crucible's non-negotiable rule — three of the reed campaign's seven rounds self-reported "merge-ready" and were wrong each time), rewrites the handoff in place, and decides whether another round is needed or the campaign has converged.

**Naming, fixed:** the pre/post role above is **`progress-judge`**, reusing the term the text-review gate's own description already uses ("run `burler` rounds → `APPROVED`/`stuck` + `progress-judge` + cap") — not "handler."
"Handler" already names a different thing in loom's existing vocabulary (the A-review→B-fix round worker itself, i.e. the "Reviewer" above) — reusing it for the targeting/validating role would collide with that.

The handoff file is the sole accumulation vehicle;
there is no live memory anywhere in the loop.
The one cost this pays versus a text-review segment today: a `progress-judge` spawn on **both** sides of the reviewer, not just post-round — a text-review segment's judge doesn't do this pre-round targeting for Discussion/Plan/Webster today;
those rounds reuse a fixed rubric, not a dynamically retargeted prompt.

### Pre-round targeting

Superseded by the `internal/treadleengine` package documentation — pre-round targeting is designed there as a general capability `Treadle`'s judge can support, exercised by Tenter's profile and simply unused by a text-review profile. See that doc's "Pre-round targeting" section instead of resolving this here.

### The handoff — two-tier memory, and the one crux

- **Handoff** — a **distilled summary**, **edited in place each round** (not appended, so per-round context stays bounded regardless of round count).
  Always read.
  The orchestrator's compressed understanding + what to target next. *(The hand-run instructions already rewrite it in place per round — this discipline is proven, not new.)*
- **Raw reviews + fixer-reports** — complete, authoritative, **read on demand** when the handoff points at something needing detail.
  Reviews inform *targeting*;
  fixer-reports inform *verification*.

The read-set is *instructions + handoff (always) + selective raw files (on demand)* — **not** "all reviews every round," which would reintroduce the O(N) context growth the handoff exists to kill.

**The one crux for going stateless (per-round respawn):** in the hand-run version a *live* thread held some things implicitly — above all "this finding has recurred before."
A respawn has no live memory, so **anything the thread knew implicitly must become explicit in the handoff.**
The prime suspect is the **finding-identity / recurrence ledger** (which findings reappeared in which rounds): if an in-place edit "cleans up" a finding that looks resolved, the recurrence trail can be silently lost and stuck-detection fails quietly.
So: **distill the prose, but keep the key-ledger lossless.**
The migration persistent-thread → respawn is essentially this one audit — find what the live thread knew implicitly and make it explicit.

### Reuse: only `Bouncer` carries over

`Tenter`'s own review-loop is expected to land as a `Shed` segment: a round producer (this module's own equivalent of the shipped `shedadapters: Burler-round producer`, wrapping whatever `Tenter`'s round mechanism turns out to be — not `burlerengine`) paired with an instance of the shipped `Bouncer: the generic review-gate producer`, the same hand-wired shape `loom`'s own review producers use (folk name "perch," see `CLAUDE.md`'s terminology note — this segment is "a perch" in that same loose sense, same shape, different round producer inside it).
Only `Bouncer` is literally reusable code here: `burlerengine`'s own round mechanism is inherently text/diff-specific (Target/Fasit/Rubric over a `shuttle` session editing text), so `Tenter`'s round producer needs its own from-scratch implementation of the same always-`Stuck`-until-approved contract, not a port of `burlerengine`.
This is the second data point (after `loom`'s own review producers) for whether `internal/treadleengine` is ever fully retired — see the shipped `Retire perch` item's own note that its retirement is a separate call, made once `Tenter` lands.

## `Hardener` — the campaign

The operator's role in the hand-run campaign was mostly **gating** — approve, ask for another round — not irreplaceable judgment.
That is front-loadable into the seed instructions ("run until the gates are green or K rounds;
do not ask").
So `Hardener` can run **autonomously, overnight**, with reed + Go handling **auto-compaction** (which, per the insight above, *is* per-round respawn).
Model rotation across rounds (Opus / Fable / Sonnet) stays as a cheap diversity lens — convergence across *different* models is stronger evidence than N passes from one.

`Hardener`'s own worktree-spawn (via `fabric`) and safe-merge-back-to-parent lifecycle is `Shed`'s job (see `internal/shedengine`'s package documentation) — the same `loom`-shared lifecycle described above, with Hardener's own Preflight (below) instead of loom's.

### The sandbox dependency

`Hardener` cannot run against the module's own repo alone — it needs a **live sandbox repo** to do destructive, stateful things (create worktrees, junctions, spawn tmux, tear down) without corrupting the real repo,
and a maintained **live-driving suite** (`tools/sandbox/SANDBOX-<MODULE>-SUITE.md`) as the substrate-exercising vehicle.
Consequences carried from the hand-run method:

- **Deploy-first.**
  The suite runs the **deployed** binary, not the working tree — re-deploy after every source change or you validate a stale binary.
- **The decisive gate is N× concurrent smoke, not a quiet serial pass** — concurrency + CPU saturation is the amplifier that surfaces teardown races and leaked substrate state.
- **Zero stray substrate state at teardown** is itself an invariant under test.
- **Grow the suite with the module** — a bug found live leaves behind both a `//go:build smoke` regression test and, where visual, a suite scenario.

## The likely `lym` shape (open)

`Tenter`'s defining trait — an accumulating, targeting review-loop — is precisely what lym's thesis otherwise *replaces* with Go.
So this probably is **not** "Go takes over the orchestrator."
More likely: **lym provides the deterministic scaffolding** and the **orchestrator brain stays an LLM** —

- **Go / lym owns** (split across `Shed` and `Treadle`): provision/reset the sandbox, deploy the binary, run the slow gates (smoke suite, zero-stray-state), collect + structure results, maintain handoff files (via `internal/state`), the per-round respawn loop, teardown.
- **LLM orch-brain owns** (Tenter's judge, within `Treadle`): read results, accumulate understanding, decide what to target next, write the next round's focused prompt.
- **`burler`-shaped round agent** (see the `internal/burlerengine` package documentation): the A→B worker, spawned per round (drives the sandbox;
  `fix-scope: source`;
  commit-per-fix).

Whether the round agent literally imports the `burler` package or only follows the same `review-prompt-template.md` discipline is an implementation choice for when this is built.

## Dependencies (tentative)

- `internal/treadleengine` package documentation — the generic round-loop engine `Tenter` would configure (as-built;
  module doc deleted per the documentation lifecycle), independent of whether `Tenter`/`Hardener` ever get built.
- `internal/shedengine`'s package documentation — the generic outer phase-FSM `Hardener` configures;
  same independence as above.
- `shuttle` — spawns the round agents and judges `Treadle`/`Tenter` drive.
- `internal/stencil` — fills the round-agent / orchestrator prompt templates (shared with `burler` and the review gate).
- `internal/state` — handoff + round artifacts on disk (the memory that makes respawn work).
- a **sandbox repo + live suite** — a provisioned environment and a maintained asset, not just code.
- `reed` transitively, via shuttle;
  possibly directly for the overnight/autonomous session + auto-compaction.

## Status / open questions

- ~~Persistent thread vs. per-round respawn~~ — resolved: per-round respawn via `Treadle`'s three-step loop (pre-round `progress-judge` → reviewer → post-round `progress-judge`);
  see above.
- ~~Naming: one module or two?~~ — resolved: `Tenter` (review-loop) + `Hardener` (`Shed` + `Tenter`, the campaign);
  see "Naming" above.
- The shared engine designs (round-runner interface, handoff/ledger format, pre-round-targeting mechanics for `Treadle`;
  the outer FSM for `Shed`) live in their own docs — not decided here, independently of whether `Tenter`/`Hardener` themselves ever get scheduled.
- Exactly what the handoff must carry losslessly (key-ledger confirmed;
  what else?).
- The Go-scaffolding / LLM-brain boundary above.
- Whether it reuses the `burler` package or just the prompt template.
- Sandbox provisioning: how much lym automates vs. a pre-existing sandbox repo.
- The treadle judge stencils (`contracts/stencils/treadle/treadle-template-judge-circling.md`, `treadle-template-judge-milestone.md`, `treadle-template-targeting.md`) are kept for Hardener but unmaintained, and are re-derived from the Bouncer judge (`bouncer/bouncer-template-judge.md`) when Hardener is built, so no dead-code sweep removes them (operator decision 2026-10-16, from the stencil intent audit of 2026-10-15).

**This module is post-loom and on-demand;
nothing here blocks the `burler → shed → loom` spine, nor the `Treadle`/`Shed` work, which proceeds independently of whether `Tenter`/`Hardener` are ever scheduled.**

entries.title: Remaining leads from the survey of comparable agent orchestrators (Oct 2026)
entries.body:
Leads borrowed from comparable open-source agent orchestrators, surveyed in October 2026 (first imported from issue #671).
Nothing here is a commitment; these are leads to triage.
The orch checked each against the code on 2026-11-17: ideas lym has built or that proved moot are dropped,
partly built ones name only what is still open, and the eight most worth doing are notes of their own in this project.
Each bullet names its source project and the lym module it would touch.

## Plan validation and concurrency (quarry, Plan-Write, board)

- **Typed scope operations on cards** (foremerge): each scope carries an additive or breaking operation,
  and deterministic rules flag colliding pairs even when files do not overlap.
  Worth comparing against board labels and the alignment gate.
- **Symbol leases between concurrent tasks** (Fusion, ORCH): expiring leases on symbol keys serialize overlapping tasks,
  with a deterministic tie-break; lym keeps overlapping tasks apart by board labels.
- **Commit-time reservation guard** (ntm): a pre-commit hook refuses a commit touching what another task holds; needs leases first.
- **Requirement-to-card traceability** (Spec Kit, Kiro): parts already name the decisions they build;
  the Plan-Write gate could also refuse a card that traces to no decision.
- **Criterion amendment ledger** (oh-my-claudecode): a card's acceptance text changes only through a recorded amendment in weft.
- **Bugfix spec with a fail-on-base test** (Kiro): a bugfix stencil for Discussion-Write,
  and a Go gate that the new test fails on the base commit and passes on the tip.

## Review (burler, Bouncer)

- **Quorum of differently-angled judges** (ccswarm): lym fans out lenses but has no quorum vote for high-risk segments.
- **Risk tier by changed paths** (yylo): globs over sensitive paths choose the review depth and the gate scope.

## Engine, recipes and governance (shed, tender, orch, board)

- **Cross-run quarantine** (Bernstein): a task that fails three times across runs is held, unless the failures were the host's.
- **Abandon as a terminal state** (Bernstein): distinct from failed, with dependents marked blocked by it.
- **Fork a run from a step with a tree snapshot** (Bernstein): `shed goto` moves the cursor but does not restore the warp tree.
- **Warm retry guarded by a workspace hash** (Bernstein): resume the native session only when the tree is unchanged.
- **Evidence reuse by input identity** (yylo): verify is skipped on the same tree; a changed review prompt could rerun only the review.
- **Recipe validator** (Conductor): route targets are checked; reachability and stencil output names are not.
- **Guidance at the next step boundary** (Conductor): a queue of operator guidance for the next producer's prompt.
- **Batched operator questions with recorded assumptions** (Spec Kit `/clarify`, Conductor): Discussion-Write asks at most a few ranked questions,
  each with a recommended answer, and records unanswered ones as assumptions.
- **Rate-limit wait**: the orch watcher wakes the orch after a usage reset; tender itself schedules no resume.
- **Standing goals and scheduled routines** (ORCH, CAO, Fusion): periodic triage, dependency bumps or `selfreport` sweeps.

## Worktrees (fabric, batten, landing)

- **Lifecycle hooks** (dmux): hub-configured hooks after pair creation and around Merge-In and landing.
- **Free a paused run's worktree** (claude-squad): commit, remove the worktree and keep the branch; the weft sibling makes it harder.

## Agent sessions (reed, shuttle)

- **Waiting-for-input signal** (agent-of-empires): shuttle has an awaiting-input state; screen heuristics still decide readiness and startup.
- **Reference status patterns and a paste pitfall** (CAO): compare its regexes and its tmux bracketed-paste note with shuttle's readiness and creel inject.
- **Context forecasting** (ntm): the orch cycles its context; Webster's Master and the loom driver do not, and nothing forecasts.
- **Staggered spawns** (ntm): space Webster forks and batten fan-out by learned rate limits.

## Observability (report, weft)

- **Hash-chained run journal** (Bernstein): a hash chain over producer outputs makes an archived run self-verifying.
- **Unverified-completion rate** (Bernstein): a `lym report` view of completions with no test or gate behind them.
- **Commit-to-record links** (AgentNote): weft links to warp by a `Warp-SHA:` trailer; a note or trailer on each warp commit could link back.
- **Run diff** (ccswarm): `lym report` comparing two archived runs' timelines and token use.
- **OpenTelemetry spans per producer** (Conductor).

## Operator attention (orch, dobby, reed)

- **Read-only web dashboard** (agent-of-empires, ralphex): a view over the board, runs and creel; Slack relay and wait marks exist.
- **Attention feed with acknowledgement states** (ntm): dobby's wait reminders have no seen, snoozed or acknowledged states.

## Discussion review (Discussion-Write, stencils, pattern)

- **Requirements-quality checklist** (Spec Kit `/checklist`): items with IDs the Discussion-review judge answers one by one.
- **Fixed analysis categories** (Kiro): inconsistency, ambiguity, conflicts, unstated assumptions and missing edge cases as named lenses.
- **PATTERN rules handed to reviewers** (Spec Kit constitution): its rules as numbered MUSTs in plan and code review prompts.
- **Glob-scoped steering** (Kiro): stencils pull per-area guidance chosen by the paths of a plan's glyphs.

entries.title: A closed area for lym: bwrap sandbox in stages, off by default
entries.brief: Run the lym process tree in a bwrap area with a host proxy and broker, built in three stages with a stop; to be split if it goes ahead
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-30)

Every agent lym starts runs with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, which many people do not accept, and a repository that states it supports safe sandboxing is worth more than one that does not.
The operator uses lym alone, on Linux (OSL-1046: Ubuntu 24.04; Neve: Kubuntu on Ubuntu 26.04, Plasma 6), and has no interest in other users or in Windows.
The research is `docs/research/platform/sandboxing-options-2026-10-30.md`: it weighs `bwrap`, Landlock, a dedicated Linux user, systemd sandboxing, podman and Claude Code's own `/sandbox`, and the packages and cards each would change.

Two exposures hold today with no area: an agent can reach `/run/user/<uid>/bus` and through it `systemd-run --user`, which starts any process outside lym's tree, and it can type into other hubs' tmux panes through their sockets in `/tmp/tmux-<uid>`, the Models hub's among them.

## Idea

Run the whole lym process tree inside a `bwrap` area launched by lym itself, with the agents free inside it and a short, controlled list of exits.
It is an option the operator turns on, never a requirement: with it off, everything works as it does today, and with it on, nothing starts when the sandbox cannot.
The operator thinks the full design is complicated and error-prone, and doubts it will work without large problems, so it is built in stages with a stop between them.
This is one large note and is split into tasks, or a project, only when the operator decides it goes ahead.

### Before the area: two cheap steps

- Start a hub's tmux server from a Konsole window, not a VS Code terminal: the server inherits the `vscode` AppArmor profile, which grants user namespaces to every agent of the hub.
- A line in `README.md` that every agent lym starts runs with bypass permissions, and that lym belongs on a machine the operator is willing to hand to its agents.

### Stage 1: the filesystem area only

`bwrap` with `--unshare-all --die-with-parent --clearenv` around reed's tmux server and everything under it, started by a new `lym area start` and a supervisor inside.

- The hub is bound read-write at its own path, since the tmux server name, the creel socket name, git's worktree links and Claude Code's transcript directory all derive from absolute paths; `/usr`, `/etc` and `/opt` are read-only, `$HOME` a tmpfs with read-only binds of the Go toolchain, the Claude Code binary and the installed `lym`.
- The area has its own Claude config directory and Go caches bound at the usual paths, with the host's plugin cache read-only on top, so the host's `settings.json` hooks never run in it.
- One host directory holds the tmux socket directory, so `lym reed attach` from outside drives the server inside; tried on OSL-1046 with a tmux server inside `bwrap`.
- `.git/hooks` is read-only; `.git/config` was to stay writable for `branch.<b>.lymLocal`, but `fabric-remote-async` removed that mark and `internal/gitrepo/branchmark.go`, so the reason is gone; whether git itself or another lym writer still needs `.git/config` writable is unchecked.
- Network stays open and there is no broker, so the landing deploy, `lym reed window`, `lym ide` and `lym hibernate request` do not work from inside; the operator does them by hand, from outside.
- A config module `area` with `required`, off by default; `lym area start` refuses on any failure and never falls back to an unsandboxed start.
- Ubuntu 24.04 needs a one-time AppArmor profile for `/usr/bin/bwrap`, loaded by root; the report names the profile, and Ubuntu 25.04 and later ship it, which is not verified on Neve.

This closes the two exposures above and shows early whether tmux, creel and dobby run well inside an area.

### Stop: the operator decides whether stage 1 works well enough to go on.

### Stage 2: egress through a host proxy

No network inside the area; a host-side proxy, reached through a bound socket, allows CONNECT to `api.anthropic.com`, `claude.ai`, `platform.claude.com`, `proxy.golang.org`, `sum.golang.org`, `github.com` and `api.github.com`, with a loopback relay inside the area.
Telemetry and the auto-updater are off by environment.
The GitHub token handed to the area is fine-grained and limited to the hub's repositories; the operator's `gh` login never enters.
WebFetch and the `prowler` skill reach only these hosts.

### Stage 3: a broker for the remaining exits

A host-side process serving a fixed set of verbs and never a command line from the area: the landing deploy (it fetches `origin/main` into its own clone, checks the commit is the tip, builds with the host's Go and installs), `lym reed window` opening Konsole, and `lym hibernate request`.
`lym ide` is refused, since VS Code on the host would run git over repositories the area writes; the host runs no git over the area's repositories at all.

## What is not claimed

Isolation from a kernel exploit, which needs a virtual machine; that data in the area cannot leave through an allowed host; and that a landed change of lym itself cannot run on the host once deployed, which matters on this hub because it develops lym.
Landlock stays a possible inner layer once both machines run a kernel with ABI 9 and 10, and Claude Code deny rules in shuttle's settings are a cheap second line inside the area; the dedicated user, podman, systemd sandboxing and Claude Code's `/sandbox` inside lym runs are left out.
The report estimates the whole at five tasks and eighteen cards.

## Related

Note `creel-cross-hub-mail`: the inbox folder sits outside an area, so reading and writing it goes through the broker.

entries.title: Codex as assistant Code-Review reviewer on real darn runs
entries.brief: Set Codex as the non-gating assistant reviewer on real runs and read what it adds beside the Claude reviewer
entries.body:
## Decision (operator, 2026-11-06)

Codex is used for review first, or as a support reviewer, not as a writer: the operator does not trust that it writes in the same tone as Claude.
The earlier idea of a writer comparison is dropped.

## Decision (operator, 2026-11-15)

LoomYard is to support Codex; this trial is not finished and stays until it reaches a verdict.

## Idea

`loom.yaml` already has `code_assist_reviewer_model`: an extra reviewer beside the Code-Review reviewer, whose report the reviewer consolidates and which never gates the round.
Set it per task through `run_settings`, as `{"loom":{"code_assist_reviewer_model":"astra[medium]"}}`, on real darn runs, and read afterwards what Codex found that the Claude reviewer did not, its false findings, and the time it added.

The benches `docs/research/codex/review/codex-code-review-bench-2026-10-28` and `codex-review-yardstick-2026-10-28` found Codex no stand-in for the Claude fan but with real findings of its own, which fits a support role.

## Results so far

Run 1, `begin-batch-wrong-conflict-kind` (`b93a0a52`), darn light, `astra[medium]` solo, no lenses, beside a `sonnet[medium]` Chair with three lenses, one round:

- Astra's one finding was real and no Claude seat had it: two test readers kept a literal beside the new constant, fixed in the landing.
  Astra filed it BLOCKING; the Chair kept it at LOW.
- Astra had no false finding, but missed both MEDIUM findings the affected-set lens found in the webster master stencil.
  It read the plan fixer's limit and judged the routing fine.
- Astra's review evidence was sound, but its sandbox could not run the gate: the runner lock under `_bolt/.lym/runproc/` was read-only.
- Time: Astra ran 11:22:27 to 11:24:36, in parallel; the Chair ended at 11:25:35, so at most a small wait on the wall clock.
  `round-<n>-usage.yaml` records no time or tokens for the assistant.

Run 2, part 1 of `codex-assist-fan-trial` (`2c4864bb`), one hand-composed `astra[medium]` run on `b93a0a52` with the three `review-code` lenses; report at `docs/research/codex/review/assist-fan-trial-2026-11-06/report.md`:

- All three lenses started and returned, and the review passed `lym burler validate-review`.
- Three MEDIUM findings, each checked against the tree and real, no false finding, 266 s, about 126,000 fresh input plus output tokens.
- Two wording points in `contracts/stencils/engine/codex/assist-fan.md`, neither blocking: it says `wait` where Astra used `wait_agent`, and "all in one go" where Astra spawned over 29 s.
  The run's change description says these were filed as notes; no such note exists, so they stand here.

Run 3, part 2 of the same task, the real composed seat beside a `sonnet[medium]` Chair with no lenses, on the report's diff, `review-code` fan asked for:

- The seat did not fan: no `spawn_agent` call, no lens report.
  It reported an instruction conflict and worked solo: the composed prompt told it to work alone and write its report "and nothing else", while the fan rules asked for lens reports.
- Two LOW findings, both real and both fixed in the landing, neither false; the Chair kept both and added a third LOW of its own.
- Time: 212 s from 13:00:44, in parallel; the Chair ended at 13:05:36, so no wait on the wall clock.
- Tokens from the Codex session: 1,326,656 in all, 1,223,680 of them cached, 5,766 out.

Billing: the weekly Codex meter moved from 0 % to 1 % during run 2 and stayed at 1 % through run 3, so the runs count against the ChatGPT plan's window and show no API billing.

Three runs are no verdict.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-06)

Task `assist-fan-seat-work-alone` (`77e7a9c7`) fixed run 3's conflict: a fanned assistant now gets a fanned seat stencil and directive, whose write surface and `output_files` name the lens reports, and "work alone" there means no other session.

On OSL-1046 a Codex assist seat read nothing: every command failed with `bwrap: setting up uid map: Permission denied`, and the Chair of `testmap-verb`'s Code-Review waited 19 minutes for the seat's end marker that never came.

Codex runs on Neve, where its sandbox works, and not on OSL-1046, where `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns` is `1` and `bwrap` cannot set up its user namespace.

`{"loom":{"code_assist_reviewer_model":"astra[medium]","code_assist_reviewer_fan":"review-code"}}` in their `run_settings`; they run on Neve.
Once all three have landed, a darn docs task reads their Code-Review rounds and gives the verdict.

## Runs chosen (operator, 2026-11-17)

Run the trial now, on the darns in flight: `redundant-literal-clause-mutants` (T5) carries the same `run_settings`, set in its running pair through `lym config loom --layer local` before its Code-Review.

Every darn the hub orch releases on Neve from here on carries them too, until the verdict.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-18)

Task `codex-assist-verdict` (`6a99d2f5`) read the 14 assistant reviews in the archived records of 12 landed darn runs and gave the verdict proposal; report `docs/research/codex/review/assist-verdict-2026-11-18/report.md`.

entries.title: Codex support in levels: review, darn, then the rest of tapestry
entries.brief: Say lym supports Codex only at a level proven on real runs; the first work is a darn-writer bench
entries.body:
## Goal (operator, 2026-11-09)

Lym can say it supports Codex only when Codex can take over what Claude does, not only as an assistant reviewer.
That is a large job, so "support" is defined in levels, and lym claims the highest level that is proven on real runs.

## Decision (operator, 2026-11-09)

This note takes the operator's wish for full support beside the decision of 2026-11-06 (note `codex-assist-review-trial`), which kept Codex to review and support and dropped a writer comparison because the operator doubted Codex writes in the same tone as Claude.
Level 2 below is where that doubt is tested, and the bench is its first work.

## Levels

1. **Review.** Codex as the non-gating assistant reviewer beside the Claude reviewer.
   Partly proven: runs and benches under `docs/research/codex/review/`; the verdict proposal of 2026-11-18 is in `docs/research/codex/review/assist-verdict-2026-11-18/report.md`, and the operator's verdict is open in `codex-assist-review-trial`.
2. **Darn.** Codex as the writer of a whole darn run that lands with no resumption.
   Open: the 2026-11-05 trial (`docs/research/codex/engine-trial/codex-engine-trial-darn-e2e-2026-11-05.md`) stopped at Darn-Write because the sandbox made the worktree's git directory read-only, so the commit was refused.
   `sandbox_mode: danger-full-access` (`codex.yaml`, set with `lym config codex --layer machine`) is built but checked by unit tests only; no real Codex session has run with it.
   Since commit `9874c966` the template default is `sandbox_mode: auto`: a launch probes the sandbox and runs `danger-full-access` itself, with a warning, on a machine whose bubblewrap cannot start, so the bench needs no hand-set mode.
   That probe path is also checked by unit tests only, until a real session runs it.
3. **The rest of the tapestry recipe.** Codex in Discussion, Plan, Plan-review and Code-Review as the main seat, and in raddle.
   Not tried; it waits until level 2 shows the quality holds.

## First work: the level 2 bench

A bench of Codex as the darn writer against Claude on one or two real darn tasks, each run once per writer.
It reads, per run: cost, review rounds, findings, wall time, and whether the run lands without a hand step.
The run also checks the open faults on the way: the skill load on a real session, and the extra reminder on an idle wake (`codex-idle-wake-extra-reminder`).
It runs as a darn task with profile `docs`, at most `high` effort for Codex, and only on the operator's go-ahead.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-15)

Task `codex-writer-bench-neve` (`c0815831`) ran the first bench run on Neve: `astra[high]` as the darn writer, replayed on the landed `ide-beam-readme-preview` (`824eb2b6`) through a bare `lym shuttle run`.
Report: `docs/research/codex/darn-writer/codex-darn-writer-replay-neve-2026-11-15/`.

- Its tree passes the gate on `./internal/ideconfig`, and its `template.yaml` and `config_test.go` match the landed change byte for byte.
- It added a documentation page the entry did not ask for, and its change description names no design decisions.
- About 4 minutes against 5 minutes 41 seconds for the landed writer, whose figure includes a 2 minute 17 second verify gate; dollar cost unknown.
- The session ran in a scratch worktree, so no board, drift or loom check ran, and it was not a whole darn run: the "lands with no resumption" test of level 2 is still open.
- It got no skills, no guards and Claude-worded stencils, so it does not count (operator, 2026-11-16).
  The operator judges level 2 after the Codex parity tasks of project `codexengine` land and the bench `codex-writer-bench` reruns on Neve, through the real producer; the OSL-1046 run is dropped.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-17)

Three of the Codex parity tasks have landed, which answers most of what the 2026-11-15 replay lacked:

- `codex-standing-instructions` (`f8cc499c`): a Codex launch carries Claude's standing items (subagent passage, deny notice, creel trust sentence, heddle passages), the user's instruction files, the skill listing and the plugin session-start contexts as `developer_instructions`.
  Its by-hand checks, a real launch with the order and content confirmed, are still open.
- `codex-question-deny-nudge` (`b2cd8150`): an autonomous Codex launch denies the question tool and gets the batching nudge through `hooks.PreToolUse` and `hooks.PostToolUse`.
- `codex-wording-engine-blocks` (`40c66912`): Claude-only wording in stencils, specs and agent-read Go text now has a Codex copy in an engine block.

So a Codex seat now gets skills, guards and Codex-worded stencils.

The rerun through the real producer has landed: task `codex-writer-bench` (`96b20f1c`), report `docs/research/codex/darn-writer/codex-darn-writer-bench-neve-2026-11-17/`.
`astra[high]` ran the real `Darn-Write` row of the darn recipe on `ide-beam-readme-preview`, and the run stopped before `Drift-Verify`; `launch-manifest-parity` landed too (`3bbc92a0`), so the report opens with both engines' manifests.

- Codex finished the fix; `template.yaml` and `config_test.go` are byte-identical to the landed ones, and its tree passes the verify gate.
- It added four lines of preview troubleshooting to `docs/overview.md` the entry did not ask for, and its change description narrates verification the description spec leaves out.
- 13 min 5 s against 5 min 41 s for the landed writer; no Codex cost, since `codexengine` has no pricer.
- No skill-load or idle-wake fault shows in the run that counts.
- The run stopped before `Drift-Verify`, so "lands with no resumption" is still unproved.

The verdict on level 2 is the operator's.

entries.title: Measure what Cortex XDR costs the test suites on OSL-1046
entries.brief: The 242 s fabricengine tier 1 against 37 to 41 s elsewhere is a machine difference no report has split
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-11-09)

Cortex XDR on OSL-1046 holds each new binary for about 10 s and scans each file a test creates, and fabricengine tests create many.
The shard report (`docs/research/speed/fabricengine-shards-2026-11-09/report.md`) put the 242 s one-process wall down to load, but the 2026-11-08 figure of 37 to 41 s was measured on another machine, so the gap is machine and Cortex, not load.
The package used 1.23 cores of 16 and `pmd` and `piud` were busy in nearly every sample.

## Idea

Separate the Cortex cost from the rest: the time a freshly built test binary waits before it runs, the time file creation takes with and without a scanned folder, and the fabricengine tier 1 wall with the repository and temp folders excluded from the scan, if the operator can have that changed.
The result says whether to cut tests, cut file and binary creation, or ask for an exclusion.

entries.title: Cut the existing redundant tests of every package, found by the coverage maps
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-11-09)

The coverage maps (`internal/testcover`, built by `lym gate test --map` since `b92c95ee`) record, per package, the blocks each tier 0 and tier 1 test covers.
The gate report (the advisory redundancy step of `lym gate test`, landed as `7f21142e`) judges only the new tests of a diff against the map;
nothing yet uses the maps to find redundant tests that already exist.
The operator wants the existing ones cut, across the packages, not only kept from growing.

The survey `redundancy-confirmed-survey` (`53d40bd0`, report `docs/research/speed/redundancy-confirmed-survey-2026-11-16/report.md`)
ran the mutation-confirmed `lym gate redundant` over 121 packages:
430 tests stay confirmed, 2.89 s of removable standalone time, and 27 of 30 sampled are false confirmations,
each asserting something its covering tests do not.
So the list is a reading filter, never a verdict:
the cut is a test-quality cleanup that reads every confirmed candidate against its covering tests, not a speed task.

## Idea

1. A candidate list per package from `lym gate redundant <package>`, which omits `//testtiming:keep` and spawn-marked tests.
2. Cut tasks on that list, each run delegating the per-test reading to subagents:
   a candidate is cut or folded into another test only when its assertions add nothing the covering tests check.
   The survey names what to look for first: absent side effects, persisted state, and inputs the covering tests do not feed.
3. `internal/fabricengine` was swept by hand on 2026-11-08, so it comes last or not at all.
4. Before judging a package, the sweep builds that package's map fresh in its own worktree with `lym gate test --map`,
   since no landing keeps the maps fresh; spawn-marked tests are neither candidates nor covers.

entries.title: Coverage maps: build them, keep them fresh, and cut the test suite with them
entries.body:
Builds the first full set of coverage maps and uses them to cut the test suite:
cut existing redundant tests.
The maps are built only on command now; the gate no longer selects tests from them.

## Order (operator, 2026-11-12)

1. Landed: the way to make the maps.
   The upkeep pass (`--upkeep`) and the prime dobby that started it were retired by `testmap-on-command` (`72b26d1a`, 2026-11-15):
   the payoff report found the pass took 7.7 to 31 minutes after a landing and saved the gate 0 to 4.2 s.
   `gate-test-map-mode` (`b92c95ee`, 2026-11-17) replaced `lym gate testmap` with `lym gate test --map`,
   which runs each test in its own process, in parallel, and writes each package's map whole.
   The maps are built only on command, and the gate runs whole packages, with no `coverage` scope.
2. Landed: the pilot on one package and the verb that lists redundant-test candidates (`lym gate redundant`, `79f0eb4a`).
   Its report is `docs/research/speed/coverage-map-pilot-2026-11-12/report.md`.
   The maps stay as the input of this verb.
3. Open: the cut stage, `redundancy-sweep-existing`.
   The operator reads the candidate lists first; the pilot found that equal coverage often hides a different assertion, so the cut stays a reading filter, not a verdict.

entries.title: Move a running task by hand-back and a fresh run, not a re-parent verb
entries.brief: The writer hands back what it knows, the run is cancelled, a new task under the new parent starts from that
entries.body:
## Seen

The study `docs/research/loom/reparent-running-task-2026-11-12.md` (commit `5e41ee2b`) finds that a verb moving a running task to another parent is feasible but wide:
two durable stores written by two modules with no atomic change, a narrow board write past the run lock,
an ancestry check on the new parent, and a cross-module tapestry run of its own.

## Idea (operator, 2026-11-15)

Moving a running task is rare, and a verb for it is clumsy for what it buys.
Instead, end the run and start a new one with more information:

1. The run's live writer writes everything it has learned to a hand-back file in its run records:
   what is done, the decisions taken, what is left, and where its commits are.
   The entry is held by the run and takes no body edit, so the file is the only place it can write.
2. The run is cancelled with `lym batten cancel`, which sets the entry back to `draft` and frees it.
   The archive tag keeps the run records, the hand-back and the commits, so the new run can read them.
3. The orch writes the hand-back into the entry's body, or into a new task under the new parent, and releases it.

What the design must settle:

- Whether the new run re-uses the old commits (a cherry-pick, which brings back the study's ancestry question) or only reads them.
- Whether this is a recipe step, a `lym batten` verb, or orch guidance alone.

The adopt redesign (`adopt-redesign`) has landed, and so has `run-fsm-tracked-records` (`27eefef6`, one run FSM over tracked records).
The project `adopt-build-resplit` has landed whole: its members `transition-push-takeover`, `machine-registry-holds-catchup`, `adopt-foreground` and `leftover-pairs-teardown` are in (`71d6ee1a`),
so the adopt work this note waited on is built.

entries.title: codexengine
entries.body:
## Goal (operator, 2026-11-03)

`codexengine` landed with project `codex-engine` and has run motif runs well, but was never tested as a whole.
A stress test proves, on real launches, that the engine does everything its design says, the hooks above all, and records each fault as a bug note.

## Codex parity (from the Sketch `codex-same-as-claude`, 2026-11-16)

A Codex session lym gives a role gets exactly what a Claude session in that role gets.
The tasks raddle filed from that Sketch build it:
`prompt-engine-per-launch`, `codex-standing-instructions`, `codex-wording-engine-blocks`, `codex-question-deny-nudge` and `launch-manifest-parity`.
The two projects `codex-engine-trial` and `codex-parity` were merged into this one (operator, 2026-11-16).

## What the engine is designed to do

The package doc `internal/shuttleengine/codexengine/doc.go` is the spec; each part below tests one area of it against real Codex sessions launched through `lym shuttle`.

1. Home and trust: the shared lym Codex home under `CODEX_HOME`, `auth.json` and sessions linked to the operator's home, `config.toml` rendered whole under a file lock, trusted roots for a worktree and a linked worktree, dropped roots for a gone folder, the read-back Warn, and the folder-trust prompt backstop.
2. Sandbox and refusals: `-a never -s workspace-write`, the records checkout as a writable root, a `.codex/rules` folder on disk, tracked by git or not, refusing the launch and a `.codex/config.toml` on disk named in a Warn (the checks read the folders on disk since `codex-trial-1-fixes`).
3. Hooks: SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, Stop with its reply, PermissionRequest and PostToolUse each reach the run's events file or activity stamp; an interrupt reads as interrupted through `turn_aborted`; the context size from `token_count`.
4. Shell guards: every installed guard row denies its command through the PreToolUse hook with its Codex steer, the prompt file carries the notices, and a hook that fails to run is seen failing open.
5. Pane and send: the composer, the busy line and the trust prompt read right; a long or multi-line send through the guarded paste-then-Enter lands whole; a dead pane after exit.
   Creel by the pane path, the only one a Codex strand has: a program's notice typed in full into an idle session, an agent's mail reminded with `run lym creel read`, and the Codex session running `lym creel read` and `lym creel post --reply` from inside its `workspace-write` sandbox, which must reach the creel daemon.
6. Skills: a `<plugin>:<name>` load reads the newest version's `SKILL.md` and the load is seen in the rollout; an unknown skill is reported unknown.
7. Stress: several Codex sessions at once, long sessions, repeated interrupts and sends, and a darn run with a Codex seat end to end.

## Rules

- Each part writes its findings to a report under `docs/research/`, and files each lym fault as a bug note on this board.
- Parts run as darn with profile `docs`, unless the operator says otherwise.
- A Codex run gets `high` effort at most.
- A Codex bench runs the real producer with only the model swapped through `run_settings`, and never hand-builds Codex's prompt. Its report opens with the run's own manifest record, from the copy kept in the run-directory root's `manifests` directory, and, for the engine that did not run, the output of `lym shuttle manifest` for the same seat (from `launch-manifest-parity`, 2026-11-17).

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-05)

Task `codex-creel-hooks` (`e3aedbc5`) gave Codex strands creel delivery through hooks, as Claude strands have: mail reaches a running session at the end of a tool call through `PostToolUse`, at a turn end through `Stop`, and an idle session through `codex queue` run by the strand's `hook-wait` waiter. So part 5's "the only one a Codex strand has" holds only for a strand opened without a prompt file (`OpenLaunch`, a standalone run), which stays a pane-mail strand.
Task `codex-creel-trial` (`afa2cf2e`, `docs/research/codex/engine-trial/codex-creel-trial-2026-11-05.md`) trialed it on real sessions in `lyt` and found one fault, filed as note `codex-idle-wake-extra-reminder`.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-07)

Task `codex-skill-load-false-missing` (`0e02aaad`) fixed a false `skill skipped ... cause="not loaded"` in part 6's load check.
`ClassifySkillLoad` now also reads a skill as loaded when a tool call output of the load turn holds the whole of its `SKILL.md`, so a seat that reads its skills through a path built at run time (a `cat .../skills/${name}/SKILL.md` loop) is no longer reported missing.
A partial output still leaves a skill missing.
The fix is checked against unit cases only: the original rollout and a live Codex run were not used, so part 6 should still see the load on a real session.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-08)

Task `codex-sandbox-mode` (`539525a0`) made part 2's sandbox a machine setting: `codex.yaml` has a `sandbox_mode` key, `workspace-write` by default or `danger-full-access`, set with `lym config codex --layer machine`.
A `danger-full-access` launch carries no sandbox flags, no network setting and no writable roots, and `OpenLaunch` does the same.
The change was checked by unit tests only.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-11)

Commit `9874c966` (task `codex-bubblewrap-sandbox`) added a third `sandbox_mode` value, `auto`, now the template default, so part 2 no longer needs the mode set by hand on a machine whose bubblewrap cannot start.
A launch under `auto` or `workspace-write` first probes the sandbox (`codex sandbox -c sandbox_mode="workspace-write" -- true` under the lym Codex home in the worktree):

- Under `auto`, a sandbox that starts runs `workspace-write`; one that refuses (OSL-1046's AppArmor-restricted user namespaces) runs `danger-full-access` with a warning naming bubblewrap's output.
- Under an explicit `workspace-write`, a sandbox that refuses refuses the launch, naming the cause and `lym config codex --layer machine --set sandbox_mode=auto`; the seat reads as not started, not stopped.
- `danger-full-access` runs no probe.

Both `Prepare` and `OpenLaunch` settle the mode through `launchSandboxMode` in `codexengine/sandbox.go`; `Prepare` refuses before `prompt.md` is written.
Part 2 therefore tests the probe, its three outcomes and the refusal on a real machine where bwrap fails (OSL-1046) and on one where it works (Neve), not only the fixed `workspace-write` flags.

entries.title: No lym check compares a map entry with a single-test coverage run
entries.brief: The trial cross-checked by hand; blocks have no line range and funcs have no profile counterpart
entries.body:
Found by the map-tooling-trial.

Nothing in lym compares a map entry with a single-test coverage run.
The trial did it by hand: `lym gate test --wait ./internal/<pkg> -- -run '^<Test>$' -count=1 -coverprofile=<abs path>`, then counted covered blocks per file in the profile against the map's `blocks` of that test grouped by file.
That agreed for both `internal/durfmt` tests and for `TestOutputs`, `TestStoreValidatesLabelsWithVocabulary` and `TestWriteSiblings` of `internal/boardengine`.

Two limits:
- The map's blocks carry file, function and hash but no line range, so the check is by count per file, not block by block.
- The map's `funcs` list (functions of linked packages a test reaches) has no single-test counterpart in a statement profile, so it is unchecked.

Add a verb, or a `--map` option, that re-measures named tests alone and reports any block or function that differs, and give blocks a line range.

Imported from [issue #144](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/144).

What happened: a loom run halted failed at the Code-Burler-Fix producer (anomaly producer-hard-failure) in round 1 attempt 1. The shedadapters guard reported that the burler twill fixer fork attempted 5 write/edit tool calls, and that a fork must never mutate a file. Way forward named by lym: inspect the target's working-tree changes, revert what the fork wrote, and resume the run. The preceding Code-Bouncer and Code-Burler-Review rows were both recorded as stuck.

Why it is abnormal: the fix round is the step meant to apply review findings, yet the fork it spawns is forbidden to write, and the fork tried anyway. Either the fixer fork's brief does not tell it that it is read-only and where to hand its fixes (so it reaches for Edit/Write), or the fix round routes work to a fork that should have been a writing session. Either way an ordinary run ends in a hard failure that needs manual revert-and-resume, and the writes may already have touched the working tree.

What to do: make the Code-Burler-Fix fork's prompt state the no-mutation contract and the channel for returning fixes, or run the fixer as a session allowed to write; and consider having the guard block or revert the fork's writes itself, or retry the attempt once with a corrective message, instead of failing the whole run.

Provenance: task slug leftover-pairs-teardown; note file loom-halt.md.

entries.title: Code-Review lets result-level issues through to PR-Review
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #139](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/139).

## Seen

A darn run (profile solid) passed Code-Review and reached PR-Review with substantive findings left: 17 items, of which the main ones were about results, not code.

- Test limits widened 10-30x without a named cause, so a golden test no longer checked the behaviour its name states (steady turning).
- Model departures kept on the strength of measurements the change itself had made obsolete.
- A set-up difference between the model and its reference (one side had a fluid torque the other lacked) that the description presented as agreement.
- No before and after figures for the comparison the task existed to move.

The PR-Review agent then has to make a full measuring and fixing round, which PR-Review is not meant for: at PR time only small things should remain.

## Why Code-Review missed it

The code reviewer reads the diff against the task and checks code quality and correctness.
It is not told to check that assertions, tolerances and measured claims in the change still hold together, and a widened limit in a test looks like an ordinary edit.

## Idea

1. Add result checks to the code reviewer's brief in every recipe, generic across hubs:
   - a widened assertion, tolerance or limit names its measured cause, or is a finding;
   - a test whose limits changed still checks what its name and doc state;
   - a claim of agreement with a reference or of an improvement carries before and after figures in the change description.
   Domain rules, such as "a kept departure from a reference model is measured on the current code", belong in the repository's PATTERN, which reviewers already get.
2. Drift compares results before and after, but a test whose limits are widened in the same change passes on both sides, so drift sees nothing.
   Let Drift also flag every assertion, tolerance or limit the change widens or removes in an existing test, and require a stated measured cause for each, as it does for a moved baseline value.
3. When PR-Review findings are more than small (by count or by a severity the reviewer gives), send the run back to Code-Review / Code-Burler instead of having the PR-Review agent fix them, and record that the earlier review missed them, so the miss is visible.

entries.title: Shuttle start: idle check misses an idle prompt, and a review strand misses its prompt turn
entries.brief: Two seat start bugs in shuttle prompt delivery
entries.body:
Two shuttle startup bugs, bundled because both sit in the prompt delivery after a seat session starts.

## Part: the idle check misses an idle prompt after skill loading

Imported from [issue #137](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/137).

### What happened

A `burler-review` seat (`code-burler-review`) failed to start twice in a row, and the loom run halted as failed with anomaly `producer-hard-failure` ("two consecutive died/timeout outcomes", attempts 1 and 1b).

Both attempts died in `shuttle` with: `deliver the prompt after loading skills: the session is not idle: strand "...": no input box is on screen; a menu or picker may be open; retry once the session is idle`, followed by `the provider never became ready`.

The pane capture embedded in the error shows the session had finished loading every skill and printed its `ok <skill names>` reply and a `done` timing line.
The last lines were an empty `❯` prompt and the `bypass permissions on` footer, which looks like an idle session with an input box.
No menu or picker is visible in the capture.

### Why it is abnormal

The session was ready for input, yet the idle check reported no input box.
Both attempts failed the same way within seconds of the skill replies (3 s and 4 s turns), so this looks like a race or a mismatch in the idle detection rather than a stuck session.
Possible causes: the check ran in the moment between the reply finishing and the prompt box being redrawn, or the check does not recognize this layout (the `✻ ... · done` line directly above the prompt).
"Retry once the session is idle" is not acted on by the seat engine: the strand is removed and the attempt counts as died, so one transient detection miss costs a full attempt and two of them halt the run.

### What to do

- Check the idle detection in the `shuttle` prompt delivery step against the saved `startup-capture.txt` of the two run dirs (`.lym/shuttle/f31a8e1cc4fffddafce3cadb9a61d6f7` and `.lym/shuttle/6c6752222111cdd03ba84620de79c3f6`).
- Make the delivery step poll for the input box for a bounded time before declaring the session not idle, instead of failing on the first miss.
- Consider that a `not idle` refusal that names "retry once idle" is retried by `shuttle` itself rather than killing the strand.

Provenance: task slug `inmemory-store-windows-root`; notes: `loom-halt.md`.

entries.title: Leftover strands and shuttle runs halt a gate re-prompt and a re-step
entries.brief: Gate re-prompt to an untracked strand, and a re-step tripping on a leftover shuttle run
entries.body:
Two bugs where a leftover strand or shuttle run stops a run, bundled because both sit in shuttle run tracking and the step that meets it.

## Part: a gate re-prompt finds its strand untracked

Imported from [issue #143](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/143).

What happened: a `lym loom run` halted as blocked at Plan-Write with anomaly `escalation-to-human`, state `stuck`.
The reason reported by lym:

```
gate failed its first check and the session was never re-prompted, since its re-prompt could not be sent: shuttle: strand "<id>" is not tracked by reed — either its run completed and was cleaned up, or reed's strand table was reset under it (a reed remove/down, or a lost or rebuilt reed.json); check "lym reed status"
```

Why it is abnormal: the gate failed, and the re-prompt to the session could not be delivered because reed no longer tracked the strand.
Nothing in the task asked for a reed reset, so either the strand was cleaned up while the producer was still running, or reed's strand table was lost or rebuilt during the run.
The run stalled for about 23 minutes before it halted, and the findings file under `.lym/shed/<slug>/gate-findings/Plan-Write.md` was left for a human.
This run followed a separate failed run in the same worktree (see the stencil include issue), so a stale or reset reed table after the earlier halt is a plausible cause.

What to do: find why the strand was untracked at re-prompt time (cleanup racing the gate, or a reed.json reset after the earlier halt).
When the strand is gone, have the gate path relaunch or resume the producer instead of halting, or fail fast with this message rather than after a long wait.

Provenance: task slug `launch-manifest-parity`; notes `loom-halt-2.md`.


## Part: a re-step halts on the shuttle run left by the interrupted stop

Imported from [issue #138](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/138).

### What happened

A `lym shed step lym-retro --until-stop` run halted `failed` at `Code-Burler-Review` with anomaly `interrupted-stop`: `loop-exited: loop ... ended without an envelope`, with no process marking the loop's exit.
The way forward in the status error was to read `loop.trace_copy` and `loop.stderr_path`, apply the interrupted rule, and re-run `lym shed step lym-retro --until-stop`.

The re-run halted the same way, again at `Code-Burler-Review`, with an identical 11-entry history and a new trace id.
The second halt's loop log carries this line:

`shuttle: a run reads running but its waiting process is gone ... strand=ly:lym-retro:code-burler-review pid=<pid>`

The pid in that warning equals the pid in the first halt's trace file name, so the run it names was left over from the first interrupted step.
The re-run found that run still reading `running`, and the loop ended without an envelope.

### Why it is abnormal

Following the way forward lym itself printed did not move the run forward: the retry tripped on the leftover from the interruption it was meant to recover from.
The history did not change between the two halts (the last entries stay `Code-Bouncer / stuck`), so the second attempt made no progress.
The note also says `Code-Burler-Review` was in flight although the last history entry is `Code-Bouncer`.

### What to do

- On a re-step after an `interrupted-stop`, reconcile a shuttle run that reads `running` whose waiting process is gone (mark it interrupted or abandoned) before starting the step, so the retry does not end on it.
- Check that the interrupted-step record names the step that was in flight, consistent with the history.
- The first loop exit left no exit marker; whether that was an actual kill or a machine stop could not be told from the notes.
  If a clean stop can look like this, record the cause where the loop exits.

Provenance: task slug `lym-retro`; notes `loom-halt.md`, `loom-halt-2.md`.

entries.title: C# hub: silent dotnet test exit, and runs failing in a hub with no tier0 or only inert changes
entries.brief: Make a refused dotnet test say so; let a hub with no tier0 or an all-inert change run and land
entries.body:
Two bugs met in the C# hub, bundled because both sit in the gate and its guard around a hub test command.

## Part: dotnet test exits 0 with no output

Imported from [issue #135](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/135).

A darn-writer agent measuring a golden test ran `dotnet test` on a C# test project.
The command exited 0 and printed nothing, not even a test count, while `lym gate test` was off limits to that agent.
The agent could not tell that no test had run and spent several rounds before noticing.
Running the built test assembly through `dotnet vstest` with a `--TestCaseFilter` ran the tests normally.

Why this is abnormal: a silent exit 0 reads as a passing run.
If a lym guard refuses or neutralises `dotnet test`, it should refuse with a message and a nonzero exit.
The darn prompt also names no way to run a single test class while measuring.

What to do:
- Make a refused or neutered `dotnet test` say so.
- Have the darn prompt name a permitted way to run one test class, for example the `dotnet vstest` route above.

Provenance: task `td-stick-slip-surface-torque`; notes Darn-Write.md.


## Part: a hub with no tier0 fails at shed build, and Finalize ignores inert_paths

Imported from [issue #133](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/133).

### Seen

In a new hub with no tests yet, a darn task with profile `docs` (drift scope off, a docs-only change) failed at once, before Darn-Write ran:

```
loomrecipe: shedbuild: producer 5 "Darn-Write": shedrecipe: Darn-Write: gate fixer: loomcli: render the Darn-Write fixer's gate call: gate config: the hub declares no tier0, so no gate has a tier to run
```

The template's gate keys all name tier `[0]`, while the template declares `tiers: {}`.
So every run in a fresh hub fails at shed build, whatever its recipe or diff.
The tackler could not fix it, since the gate config is written only from the prime, and it handed the stop back.

### Workaround

From the prime, declare a tier0 and mark docs as inert:

```
lym config gate --layer default --set 'tiers.tier0={command: "dotnet test {targets} {args}", all_targets: ., timeout_min: 30, counter: vstest}' --set scoper=dotnet --set 'inert_paths=["*.md", "docs/*"]'
```

### Expected

A hub with no declared tiers can run a docs-only task: either the gate call is rendered only when a tier is needed,
or a gate key naming no declared tier passes with nothing to run.
At least, hub setup or the first release should flag the missing tier0 before a run starts, instead of a failed run and a tackler attempt.


### Issue comment, 2026-11-16

### Seen: Finalize ignores `inert_paths`

After the workaround above, the same docs-only darn run reached Finalize, and its landing gate failed with no failing test.
The branch held only `README.md` and a file under `docs/`, both covered by `inert_paths: ["*.md", "docs/*"]`.
Finalize still ran tier0 over all targets (gate key `finalize`, scope `all`), and in a repository with no .NET project yet,
`dotnet test .` exits with MSB1003 "Specify a project or solution file".
The Finalize fixer could not fix it on the task branch without adding code outside the task's bounds.

### Workaround

From the prime, make tier0 pass when no project exists:

```
lym config gate --layer default --set 'tiers.tier0.command=bash -c '"'"'if ls *.sln *.slnx *.csproj >/dev/null 2>&1; then dotnet test {targets} {args}; else echo no .NET project, nothing to test; fi'"'"''
```

### Expected

A change whose files are all inert runs no tier at any gate key, Finalize included,
or a scope-`all` gate in a repository with nothing to test passes instead of failing the landing.

entries.title: selfreport -b takes a file path as the body text, losing the report
entries.brief: An agent passed a file path to -b and the issue body became the path
entries.body:
An agent filed issue #136 with `lym selfreport create "<title>" -b .scratch/selfreport-missing-brief.md`.
`-b` takes the body text, so the issue body became the path and the report itself was lost.

Idea: give `lym selfreport create` a `--body-file <path>` flag (with `-` for stdin), and refuse or warn when `-b` text is a single line naming an existing file.

entries.title: Seed-IDE fails: records push calls main-weft ended on origin
entries.brief: A new run fails at Seed-IDE because the prime records branch is read as ended on origin; a rerun passes
entries.body:
## Seen

Twice on 2026-11-18 a newly started batten run failed at Seed-IDE, right after Open-Window, with:

```
fabricengine: push records side at /home/knatte/Code/loomyard-LYMHUB/loomyard-weft: the entry of branch main-weft is ended on origin, so the branch was not pushed and is left to its teardown
```

It hit `retro-stencil-fixes` in the morning and `shuttle-start-idle-and-prompt` at 09:01Z, while other runs released in the same batch started cleanly.
The branch it names is the prime records branch `main-weft`, which is never ended; the message comes from `recordsSideNotLanded` in `internal/fabricengine/pushanchored.go`.

## Workaround

The orch reran `lym batten run <slug>`; the run then went on through Run-Shed.

## Expected

A push of the prime records side never classifies `main-weft` as ended on origin, and a transient classification does not fail the run at Seed-IDE.
